newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: FEATURE-Death penalty debate rages in Puerto Rico.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Death penalty debate rages in Puerto Rico.

text.p: A constitutional showdown is looming between Washington and Puerto Rico over U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno's approval of the death penalty for an accused killer on the island.

Reno in January gave federal prosecutors authority to seek the death penalty for Ian Rosario-Melendez, who is accused of killing security guard Angel Garcia during a December 1995 bank robbery near San Juan.

The case was the first in the U.S. commonwealth to be affected by a provision in President Bill Clinton's 1994 crime legislation that allows the federal government to seek the death penalty for homicides committed during bank robberies. The issue strikes at the very heart of the often-ambiguous relationship between the United States and its largest territory, a Spanish-speaking Caribbean island of 3.7 million.

Although federal prosecutors have not yet decided whether to seek capital punishment for Rosario-Melendez, protests are growing. Puerto Rico, which was colonised by Spain in the 16th century, has a long Catholic tradition and the death penalty faces broad opposition.
Puerto Rico's 1952 constitution prohibits capital punishment and lawmakers say the United States cannot legally carry out an execution here -- a claim that is still to be tested in the courts.

The Rosario-Melendez case has been followed by several others. Prosecutors this month submitted two to Reno for death penalty authorisation and Assistant District Attorney Edwin Vazquez said four more potential death cases were pending.

Representative Jorge de Castro submitted a resolution in the island's legislature demanding that Reno declare Puerto Rico exempt from the death penalty. He also wrote to the attorney general, arguing that "We have a special relationship with the United States and certain federal laws don't apply here."
De Castro and colleagues in the Popular Democratic Party say the terms of the island's commonwealth status protect it from federal interference in matters like the imposition of the death penalty.

Puerto Ricans are U.S. citizens but do not pay federal taxes, although they receive billions of dollars each year in welfare and food stamps. The island has a non-voting resident commissioner in the U.S. House of Representatives. Residents can vote in party presidential primaries but are barred from voting in general elections for president.

"We have a consensus against the death penalty but (statehood supporters) don't want to go along with it because they say we are a colony and have to do what the federal government says," de Castro charged.
PUERTO RICAN LAW SEEN SUBSERVIENT TO U.S.

Members of the ruling New Progressive Party, which seeks statehood for Puerto Rico, say commonwealth status is colonialism and contend there is nothing to protect Puerto Rico from federal imposition of capital punishment.

"Generally most statehooders, including myself, are against the death penalty," New Progressive Party Sen. Kenneth McClintock-Hernandez said. "But there's nothing we can do about it once Reno gives the authorisation. Puerto Rico's constitution is nothing more than a federal document and our law is subservient to federal law."
The issue may come down to a constitutional fight, but all sides agreed any attempt to execute someone in Puerto Rico would be costly.

"Both the Catholic and Protestant churches have strongly opposed the death penalty throughout the last century. That has only solidified the Puerto Rican consciousness against capital punishment," the Rev. Moises Rosa, executive secretary of Puerto Rico's Evangelical Council, said.
"After they go through all the lawsuits, appeals and protest, it will cost them $10 million to put someone to death in Puerto Rico," he added.
